<reflection>
- The first experiment resulted in very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values across all 20 candidate mechanisms (ranging from -24.27 to -22.78). This indicates that under moderate, standard conditions (S=2.0, cat=0.05, P=0.0), all models have enough flexibility to fit the baseline kinetic profile.
- My aim to establish a baseline was achieved, but it did not significantly separate the models. We now need to apply more extreme or specific perturbations to break this degeneracy.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
Since all models can mimic standard kinetics under the baseline conditions, we must introduce conditions that selectively trigger specific mechanistic features. By adding a significant initial concentration of product (P = 0.5), we can strongly differentiate mechanisms involving product-induced deactivation or product inhibition (M12, M17, M5) from those that do not. If the true mechanism involves product deactivation, the reaction will be significantly slower or halt earlier than predicted by models without it. Furthermore, by increasing the catalyst concentration (cat = 0.15) and using a moderate substrate concentration (S = 1.0), we increase the relative rate of bimolecular catalyst interactions (M2, M3, M13, M18, M19) compared to unimolecular steps. This combination of high catalyst and initial product will force models with these specific higher-order or product-dependent terms to diverge from the standard Michaelis-Menten (M1) and unimolecular deactivation models (M9, M14).
</hypothesis>
